findings.title: No code implements the 'Mean score' condensation; 2 of 4 Table 1 rows untraceable
findings.claim: Every place that condenses an author's per-paper cosine similarities into one user-paper score uses max only (experiment_utils.py:22 np.max; tfidf_authors.py:71 and sentence_transformer_authors.py:39 both `.max(axis=0)`); no code computes the 'mean of the cosine similarities' the paper describes for the Mean-score models.
findings.concern: The 'Mean score, TF-IDF' and 'Mean score, Sentence transformer' rows of Table 1 (and the corresponding appendix tables) cannot be reproduced from the committed code, yet the committed notebook's own output (coef 16.2482, z 66.148, pseudo-R² 0.09085) exactly matches Table 1's Mean-score Sentence-transformer row — showing a mean-condensation pipeline was run but is absent from the repo.
findings.resolution: Add the mean-condensation code path (mean over the author's training papers) used to produce the Mean-score rows, or clarify how those rows were generated.

findings.title: cvxpy (core optimizer) plus matplotlib and seaborn missing from requirements.txt
findings.quote:
import numpy as np
import cvxpy as cp
findings.claim: The entire two-sided-fairness optimization that generates the empirical tradeoff curves depends on cvxpy (twosf_solver.py) and the SCS solver, but requirements.txt (44 pinned packages) lists neither cvxpy nor matplotlib (used by all fig*.py and the notebook) nor seaborn (notebook).
findings.concern: The pinned environment cannot run any of the paper's empirical experiments or reproduce any figure, because the solver and plotting libraries are absent from the dependency specification.
findings.resolution: Add cvxpy (and its SCS backend), matplotlib, and seaborn with the versions used to requirements.txt.

findings.title: No committed script builds the {authors,papers} embedding pickle that fig2a/fig2b consume
findings.claim: fig2a.py/fig2b.py load their `--df` input via load_data, which expects a pickled dict with 'authors' (list of dicts each holding an 'embedding') and 'papers' (paper embeddings); the recommendation scripts only emit scipy-sparse TF-IDF matrix pickles (tfidf_authors.py:41,45) and CSVs, never this dict.
findings.concern: The empirical price-of-fairness figures (Fig. 3a/3b), the paper's core empirical result, cannot be regenerated from the committed pipeline because the data-preparation step that converts embeddings into the figure-input pickle is absent.
findings.resolution: Provide the script that builds the {authors,papers} embedding pickle from the arXiv/embedding pipeline, or commit an example pickle.

findings.title: Intro '>47% of papers <0.0001% recommendation probability' has no generating code
findings.quote: for arXiv prepints, we find that on average more than 47% of papers have less than a 0.0001% probability of being recommended to any user, even when the number of users and items are the same.
findings.claim: This introductory quantitative claim requires computing per-item recommendation probabilities/exposure under a recommendation policy; a repo-wide search finds no script that computes any item recommendation probability or exposure statistic (the only '0.47' in the repo is an unrelated statsmodels quasi-separation warning).
findings.concern: A specific quantitative claim used to motivate the paper cannot be traced to any computation in the repository.
findings.resolution: Point to (or add) the script that computes per-item recommendation probabilities and the 47% / 0.0001% figure.

findings.title: tfidf_authors.py writes the last author's similarity scores onto every row
findings.claim: Inside the per-author loop, `similarity_score` for the whole accumulated `all_recommendations` frame is rebuilt by title-lookup against the current author's `scores_per_paper` and reassigned each iteration; because `scores_per_paper` covers all test-paper titles, after the final iteration every row (including earlier authors') carries the LAST author's similarity for that paper title.
findings.concern: The `recommendations_authors_method.csv` produced by the main-text TF-IDF model has a corrupted `similarity_score` column, so re-running the committed script will not reproduce Table 1/Table 3's 'Max score, TF-IDF' validation (sentence_transformer_authors.py:58 assigns the score correctly per row, so only the TF-IDF path is affected).
findings.resolution: Assign `similarity_score` inside `recommend_papers` per (author,paper) as sentence_transformer_authors.py:58 does (using avg_cosine_sim directly), not by post-hoc title matching in the loop.

findings.title: Table 1/3 'Adjusted R2' is actually statsmodels McFadden Pseudo-R²
findings.claim: The regression is a statsmodels Logit (notebook cell 26 `smf.logit`), whose summary reports a McFadden 'Pseudo R-squ.' (visible in the committed cell-27 output as 'Pseudo R-squ.: 0.09085'); the paper's Table 1 and Table 3 label this column 'Adjusted R2'.
findings.concern: An adjusted R² is not defined for logistic regression; the reported values are McFadden pseudo-R², so the column label is misleading though the underlying number is a valid pseudo-R².
findings.resolution: Relabel the column 'McFadden Pseudo-R²' (or state the pseudo-R² variant used).

findings.title: Committed driver caps authors at 1000 and notebook regresses ~2000 papers/user, vs paper's 1,128 users × 14,307 papers
findings.quote:
num_authors_to_select = min(1000, len(unique_full_names))
authors_list = random.sample(sorted(unique_full_names), num_authors_to_select)
findings.claim: The recommendation drivers sample at most 1000 authors (tfidf_authors.py:141, sentence_transformer_authors.py:88), yet Appendix B.3 reports evaluating 1,128 users and 14,307 papers; the committed notebook that reproduces a Table-1 row runs on 2,256,000 observations (= 1,128 users × ~2,000 papers), not 1,128 × 14,307.
findings.concern: The scale actually implemented/committed does not match the evaluation scale described in the paper, so the committed artifacts do not reproduce the reported Table 1 sample.
findings.resolution: Reconcile the author cap and the per-user paper count with the reported 1,128 users × 14,307 papers evaluation, or document how the committed run relates to the paper's numbers.

findings.title: Citation-validation significance rests on ~2.26M non-independent user-paper pairs with nonrobust SEs
findings.quote: In Table 1 we show the results of a logistic regression between each similarity score and the presence of a citation, where the coefficient on the score is large and statistically significant for each model
findings.claim: The logistic regression (notebook cell 26 `smf.logit`, 'Covariance Type: nonrobust', 'No. Observations: 2256000') treats every user-paper pair as an independent observation, but each of the ~1,128 users contributes ~2,000 correlated rows and each paper recurs across users, so the pairs are strongly clustered.
findings.concern: With unclustered standard errors on massively non-independent rows, the reported z-values (66–212) and p<0.001 overstate significance by orders of magnitude; the effective sample size is far smaller than 2.26M, so 'statistically significant' is not supported even though the positive association is plausibly real (cited papers average 0.696 vs 0.613 similarity).
findings.resolution: Refit with standard errors clustered by user (and/or paper), or aggregate to per-user statistics; report effect sizes rather than relying on p-values driven by pair count.

findings.title: No RNG is seeded anywhere; subsampling, clustering, and author selection vary run-to-run
findings.quote:
def sample_utility(m, n, sample_m,sample_n,W):
    rng = np.random.default_rng()
    
    users = rng.choice(m, size=sample_m, replace=False)
    items = rng.choice(n, size=sample_n, replace=False)
findings.claim: Every stochastic step is unseeded: sample_utility uses a fresh np.random.default_rng() per call, KMeans (fig2a.py:22) has no random_state, and the recommendation drivers use random.sample without seeding (tfidf_authors.py:142).
findings.concern: The reported curves (means over 10 random samples) and the sampled author/paper sets cannot be reproduced exactly, hampering verification of the empirical figures and Table 1's specific values.
findings.resolution: Expose and record a random seed for numpy, python random, and KMeans so runs are reproducible.

findings.title: rec_referenced_by_author indexes refs_dict by s2PaperId without a membership guard
findings.quote:
filt_data = refs_dict[rec_row['s2PaperId']]
filt_paper_ids = [ref['Reference Paper ID'] for ref in filt_data]
findings.claim: refs_dict is built only from Source Paper IDs present in pulled_references; a recommended paper whose s2PaperId has no pulled references (or a NaN/missing id) is not a key, so `refs_dict[rec_row['s2PaperId']]` raises KeyError.
findings.concern: If any recommended paper lacks pulled references, the whole evaluation loop crashes; whether this triggers depends on data I cannot run, hence a question.
findings.resolution: Use refs_dict.get(rec_row['s2PaperId'], []) and confirm every recommended paper had references successfully pulled.
